title: Advertisement of Multiple Paths in BGP
summary: This standards-track RFC defines a BGP extension for advertising multiple paths for the same prefix without the new ones replacing the old. Each path is identified by a Path Identifier in addition to the prefix.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of telling a neighbor only your best route, you list several, each with its own tag.

questions: what is a bgp path identifier
subtitle: How BGP speakers can advertise several paths to the same prefix without each one replacing the last.

tldr.problem: Base BGP lets a speaker advertise only one path per prefix, because a new advertisement for the same NLRI implicitly replaces the old one.
tldr.mechanism: Each path gets a four-octet Path Identifier prepended to its NLRI, and peers agree to use it through the ADD-PATH capability (code 69).
tldr.outcome: Extra paths can help reduce or eliminate persistent route oscillations and give alternate or backup paths for better routing and faster convergence.

facts.label: Capability tuple
facts.value: AFI (2 octets), SAFI (1 octet), Send/Receive (1 octet)

today: RFC 7911 is a Proposed Standard from July 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: One Path per Prefix Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The BGP specification, RFC 4271, has an Update-Send Process that advertises the routes chosen by the Decision Process. It makes no provision for advertising multiple paths for the same address prefix, also called the same Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI). A route with the same NLRI as an earlier route implicitly replaces it.

This RFC defines an extension that removes that limit. The essence is that each path is identified by a Path Identifier in addition to the address prefix.

The RFC says the extra paths can help reduce or eliminate persistent route oscillations. They can also help with optimal routing and convergence by providing alternate or backup paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, telling your neighbor a new route to a place made them forget the old one. This extension lets you tell them about many routes at once.

sections.title: Identifying a Path
sections.content:
In BGP a path is the information in the Path Attribute field of an UPDATE message. Since base BGP allows one path per prefix, a path can be keyed on the prefix alone. To carry several, a path must be identified by the pair of the prefix and a Path Identifier.

Path Identifier assignment is a purely local matter, but it MUST let the speaker use the (Prefix, Path Identifier) pair to uniquely identify a path advertised to a neighbor. A speaker that re-advertises a route MUST generate its own Path Identifier for it. A receiver should not assume the identifier carries any particular meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: Each route gets a name tag that only the sender cares about. The tag just keeps routes to the same place from getting mixed up.

sections.title: Extended NLRI Encoding
sections.content:
To carry the identifier in an UPDATE, the NLRI encoding MUST be extended by prepending a Path Identifier field of four octets. The rest of the entry is the usual one-octet length and the variable-length prefix.

The extended encoding is used only as described in the operation section, that is, when both sides have agreed to it.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing the name tag in front of the address on each envelope.

sections.title: The ADD-PATH Capability
sections.content:
ADD-PATH is a BGP capability as defined in RFC 5492, with Capability Code 69. Its length is variable, and its value is one or more tuples of an Address Family Identifier (2 octets), a Subsequent Address Family Identifier (1 octet) and a Send/Receive field (1 octet).

The Send/Receive value says what the sender can do for that AFI/SAFI: 1 means it can receive multiple paths, 2 means it can send them, and 3 means both. Any other value SHOULD cause the capability to be treated as not understood and ignored. A speaker supporting several AFI/SAFIs MUST list them all in a single instance of the capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the name tags, each side says whether it can send tagged routes, receive them, or both.

sections.title: How Multiple Paths Are Sent
sections.content:
Apart from allowing multiple paths, the advertisement rules of RFC 4271 do not change. A new advertisement for a given prefix and Path Identifier replaces the earlier one for that same pair. A withdraw for a Path Identifier not seen before SHOULD be silently ignored.

To send multiple paths for an AFI/SAFI, a speaker MUST advertise the capability with Send/Receive of 2 or 3 and MUST receive it from the peer with a value of 1 or 3. Only then does it generate updates keyed on prefix and Path Identifier using the extended encoding. Otherwise it follows RFC 4271.

When more than one path is advertised to a neighbor, a speaker SHOULD include the best route, unless that path was received from that neighbor. Because identifiers are local and may not survive a control plane restart, implementations SHOULD take special care that the forwarding plane of a Receiving Speaker (see RFC 4724) is not affected during graceful restart.
sections.plainLanguage: Tagged routes are only used if one side can send them and the other can receive them. A new route with the same tag replaces the old one with that tag, and routes with other tags stay.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that care is needed to keep routing and forwarding consistent in a network, and points to separate best-practice guidance.

The only explicit sign that the extended encoding is in use on a session is the capability exchange. A packet analyzer looking at a live session may therefore fail to decode the UPDATEs, since it lacks knowledge of the exchanged capabilities.

A provider edge or peering router facing external neighbors usually advertises at most one path to internal neighbors. If it advertises more and extra information is needed, it could use attributes such as the Edge_Discriminator attribute, which is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: If you peek at the mail without knowing about the name tags, it looks like gibberish. Careful setup keeps everyone's maps consistent.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Multiple paths for many prefixes may reach a speaker, potentially depleting memory or even causing network-wide instability, which can be considered a denial-of-service attack. The RFC notes this is not a new vulnerability but one present in base BGP. Users are encouraged to study best practices before use, and the security concerns of base BGP also apply.

IANA assigned value 69 for the ADD-PATH Capability in the Capability Codes registry.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sends you a mountain of routes, your router could run out of room. That risk already existed, but this extension can make the pile bigger.
